stances.claim: The US Electoral College system is not 'undemocratic' merely because the popular-vote winner has lost the electoral vote five times (1824, 1876, 1888, 2000, 2016) -- democracy 'has many faces depending on a country's history, traditions, and aspirations.'

The Electoral College's enduring resistance to amendment (unchanged since 1789) is structural protection of state autonomy: Article V deliberately makes amendment 'extremely difficult' because the US was founded by European immigrants who 'zealously guarded their autonomy' and ceded only defense, diplomacy, and relevant taxation to the federal government.

The bicameral design -- Senate's state-equality (2 senators per state regardless of population) balanced by House's population-apportionment -- produces a 'democratic' Union in the same way the UN's sovereign equality (each member one vote regardless of population) produces a democratic international order.

Comparative-process evidence: indirect election of British prime ministers by Parliament and direct election of Philippine presidents by mere plurality are also not undemocratic -- 'as shown repeatedly by poll surveys, the majority of the people unite post-election and support the elected top official.'

The simplest test of any election process is Lincoln's 'government of the people, by the people and for the people' -- to which CJ 'respectfully add[s]... under the rule of law' as the cross-cultural democracy criterion.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with a FLASH announcement -- congratulating retired Senior Justice Antonio T. Carpio on the University of the Philippines's conferment (Dec 10) of an honorary Doctor of Laws, with CJ and his wife Leni attending online -- then turns to the question of whether the US election system that elected Trump in 2016 and repudiated him in 2020 is 'undemocratic.' He explains the indirect structure: voters elect 538 members of the Electoral College who in turn elect the president, with state legislatures determining the process by local law (typically supervised by a state secretary of state, a political appointee). The popular-vote-vs-electoral-vote mismatch has occurred five times (1824, 1876, 1888, 2000, 2016 -- including Clinton's three-million-vote popular-vote win lost to Trump 304-227). The structure is locked in by Article V of the US Constitution (1789), which makes amendment 'extremely difficult' -- requiring either two-thirds of both chambers proposing followed by three-fourths-of-states (38 of 50) ratification, or two-thirds of state legislatures requesting a constitutional convention followed by three-fourths ratification. The framers built this difficulty to 'protect state autonomy,' because European immigrants 'zealously guarded their autonomy (or self-rule), ceding only or mostly their defense needs and diplomatic dealings with the outside world (plus relevant taxation) to their federal government.' Autonomy also explains the 100-member Senate (two per state regardless of population) -- counterweighted by population-proportional House representation. CJ argues that this state-equality-with-popular-balance arrangement makes the Union 'democratic in the same way that the sovereign equality of independent states in the United Nations gives every member one vote regardless of population.' Comparative-process examples -- indirect election of British PMs by Parliament, direct election of Philippine presidents by mere plurality -- show 'democracy has many faces depending on a country's history, traditions, and aspirations.' The simplest test, he concludes, is adherence to Lincoln's 'government of the people, by the people and for the people' -- to which he 'respectfully add[s]... under the rule of law.'
